card.title: I want to know what made a couple book, as well as what they loved afterward
card.series: Watch Us Build an Ad Strategy
card.audience: Wedding pros with strong reviews who want their advertising to reflect why their best-fit couples chose them.
card.why_selected: This earns the reach piece through a clear founder perspective rather than a forced polarizing hook. It differs from the recent UVP training: the point is which customer evidence WIA wants and why, rather than the general importance of positioning before campaign setup.
card.wia_in_action: In a conversation with the team about improving WIA's own marketing, Whitney explained that WIA asks new ELEVATE clients whether they have research on why couples book them. She floated asking newly booked couples about their decision and using what WIA learns in ad copy and landing pages. It is an idea WIA is exploring, not a process clients receive today.
card.why_it_matters: An owner may think, 'Our reviews already tell you why couples love us.' Whitney's question makes room for another kind of evidence: what mattered to the couple before the wedding happened, while they were still deciding. It does not dismiss reviews or claim an industry-wide research gap.
evidence_points: Whitney said WIA asks new ELEVATE clients whether they have market research to share.
She distinguished reviews from research into buying triggers.
She proposed asking newly signed clients about their decision and feeding that information back into ad copy and landing pages.
The call does not report survey responses or changes made from that research.
card.core_perspective: I want to understand what a couple was weighing when they chose your business. Their review can tell us what they loved about the experience. Asking about the booking decision can give us different information to consider when we write your ads.
card.offer_connection: This shows the thinking behind ELEVATE's messaging and advertising work. Keep the piece focused on the value of asking about the booking decision, with no offer CTA and no promise that a survey workflow is included or live.
verify_before_publishing: Approve use of Whitney's historical call remarks; avoid her broad characterization of wedding pros as a measured finding.
Describe the client survey and shared-data workflow as proposed, not implemented or currently included.

email.opening:
Hi {{contact.first_name}},

In a team conversation about our own marketing, I brought up something I want to understand about the wedding businesses we advertise: what helped their couples decide to book?
email.preview: What couples loved afterward and what mattered when they chose you are both worth understanding.
email.argument: Begin with the value of strong reviews and the owner's desire to represent that experience well in advertising. Explain that a question about the booking decision looks at an earlier moment, when the couple was still weighing their options. Describe WIA asking new ELEVATE clients whether they have market research to share. Then introduce Whitney's historical proposal to ask newly booked couples about their choice and consider what WIA learns in ad copy and landing pages. Keep it in flowing paragraphs, with no survey mechanics, invented responses or reported outcomes.
email.transformation: Help the reader see two useful perspectives on their value: what couples appreciate after working with them and what matters before choosing them. Connect that distinction to how WIA decides what to communicate in advertising.
subject_options: What made your couples decide to book?
A question I ask alongside reading reviews
Understanding the choice before the wedding

reels.job: Introduce Whitney's curiosity about the booking decision and show the WIA contribution through her historical team discussion. One new talking-head script, not a cut assembled from the supplied excerpts.
beats: A strong review gives us something useful: the couple's description of what they loved about working with you.
When we're getting to know a new ELEVATE client, we also ask whether they have research to share about why couples book.
In a team conversation about our own marketing, I proposed asking newly booked couples about that decision. What were they weighing, and what helped them feel ready to choose the business?
Those answers could give us different information to consider in ad copy and landing pages. This was a proposal, so we're sharing the thinking rather than reporting survey findings.
Close with the principle: I want our advertising to reflect what matters to a couple while they're deciding, as well as the experience they'll have afterward. No offer or engagement ask.
reels.spoken_opening: I'd like to know what your couples were considering before they ever had an experience to review.

caption.adds: Develop a companion caption using Savannah's framework. Start with the owner's desire for ads that reflect their value. Respect reviews as evidence of the delivered experience, then explain the additional booking-decision question. Use Whitney's internal proposal to show how WIA connects that curiosity to ad copy and landing pages. Add depth to the Reel rather than repeating its opening, cover or sequence. No invented couple answers and no offer mechanics.
caption.hook: There's useful information in the choice a couple makes before their wedding day.
caption.ending: Finish on the distinction between understanding the choice and understanding the experience. No explicit ask. Sign off as Whitney.

carousel.job: Make the distinction between experience feedback and decision research tangible, then explain how Whitney proposed using the latter in WIA's advertising work.

slides.job: Open with two moments worth understanding.
slides.text: Your couples' reviews tell one part of the story. I'm also interested in what happened while they were deciding whether to book you. Those two moments give us different things to consider when we write your ads.

A thoughtful review can tell us what a couple loved about their experience with your business. That's valuable language to understand and consider in advertising. I also want to make room for a question about how they chose you in the first place.

While a couple is choosing a vendor, what are they weighing? What matters enough to influence their decision? Asking about that moment gives us a way to explore their choice directly, alongside what they loved afterward.

When we onboard a new ELEVATE client, we ask whether they have market research to share. We want to understand the business through its clients' decisions as well as its own description of what it offers. That question helps shape what we're curious about as we develop the advertising.

In an internal team conversation about our own marketing, I proposed asking newly booked couples about their decision. The idea was to learn from them soon after they'd chosen the business. It was a proposal, rather than a set of survey findings.

slides.job: Connect the information to WIA's advertising work.
slides.text: I wanted us to consider what we learned when writing ad copy and landing pages. A couple's answer could help us decide which parts of the business deserve emphasis. We'd be working from information about their choice, rather than assuming we already knew what mattered.

slides.job: Close on the principle without an ask.
slides.text: For me, these questions belong together: what did the couple value in their experience, and what mattered when they chose you? Each looks at a different part of the relationship. Understanding both gives us more to consider when we communicate your value to the next couple.

approved_angle.title: I want to know what made a couple book, as well as what they loved afterward
approved_angle.core_perspective: I want to understand what a couple was weighing when they chose your business. Their review can tell us what they loved about the experience. Asking about the booking decision can give us different information to consider when we write your ads.

intended_shift.do: Consider what they know about their couples' booking decisions and what they would like to ask a newly booked couple. No public engagement or offer ask.
intended_shift.believe: WIA's advertising work involves understanding the reasons couples choose a business, as well as representing the experience it delivers.
intended_shift.understand: What couples loved after their wedding and what mattered while they were choosing a vendor are different questions. Both can inform how a business communicates its value.

body.wia_perspective: In an internal team conversation about our own marketing, I brought up a question we ask new ELEVATE clients: do they have any research about why couples chose them? Reviews are useful evidence of the experience a business delivers. I also want to understand the decision that came before that experience. What was the couple weighing, and what helped them feel ready to book? I proposed asking newly booked couples about that decision and considering their answers when we write ad copy and landing pages. That remains an idea to explore. The principle is the part worth sharing: understanding what matters to your couples gives us more to work with when we communicate why they should choose you.

before_publishing.text: Confirm Whitney's attribution and approval for public reuse of these historical remarks.
Keep the survey idea a historical proposal. Do not describe a live or included LeadLock workflow.
Do not claim survey responses, changes to advertising or performance improvements. None are reported.
Omit the broad claim that wedding pros never have research. It is not a measured finding.
Confirm no explicit ask at Gate 2 and approve copy before developing visuals.

narrative_outline.cta: No explicit ask. End on the value of understanding the decision, without naming an offer as the next step.

hooks.text: When we're getting to know a wedding business, I want to understand the moment a couple decided to book.
What mattered to your couples while they were still choosing between you and their other options?
I think the booking decision deserves as much curiosity as the glowing review afterward.

narrative_outline.main_point: A review and a question about the booking decision look at different moments. Asking about both gives WIA different evidence to consider when communicating a wedding business's value.
narrative_outline.transformation: The owner starts considering both the experience their business delivers and the reasons a couple felt ready to choose it. WIA's messaging work becomes more concrete: understanding the couple before deciding what to emphasise in advertising.
problems_desires_symptoms: You have thoughtful reviews that describe the experience you deliver, and you want your ads to reflect that value.
You also want to understand which parts of your business mattered to couples before they had experienced your work.
The useful question is what helped a best-fit couple choose you while they were still considering their options.

strategic_purpose.why_now: Show the thinking behind WIA's messaging work through a specific question owners can recognise. Within Watch Us Build an Ad Strategy, this introduces how WIA looks for evidence about a couple's decision, without repeating campaign diagnosis or pre-tour nurture content.

supporting_example.scene: During a historical internal team conversation about improving WIA's own marketing, Whitney described asking new ELEVATE clients whether they had market research to share. She distinguished the reviews clients offered from information about buying decisions, then floated asking newly signed clients about their choice.
supporting_example.wia_move: Whitney proposed gathering booking-decision information and bringing what WIA learns into ad copy and landing pages. The brief uses her reasoning, not the proposed survey mechanics, as the example of WIA's work.
supporting_example.client_contribution: No client participated in this scene, and no couple's response is supplied. Whitney originated the proposal. The record does not establish that surveys were sent or that any advertising was changed.

prior_content_context.argument: I want to understand what a couple was weighing when they chose your business. Their review can tell us what they loved about the experience. Asking about the booking decision can give us different information to consider when we write your ads.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding pros with strong reviews who want their advertising to reflect why their best-fit couples chose them.
prior_content_context.mechanism: During a strategy call, Whitney explained that WIA asks ELEVATE clients for existing buying research. She proposed collecting feedback from newly booked couples and using what WIA learns to inform ad copy and landing pages. The WIA move is customer research tied to a specific advertising decision.

prior_content_context.argument: We want enough evidence to make a useful recommendation. In office hours, Carmen considered how much traffic a venue campaign had received, looked at what visitors were doing after the click and recommended Jacqueline's feedback on the landing page. She kept the open questions open.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding venue owners who want expert guidance on what to keep running, what to review and when to make a change.
prior_content_context.mechanism: Carmen used diagnosis beyond the dashboard. She considered the limited traffic, discussed different kinds of visitor behavior and avoided claiming a cause. When a visitor reached the inquiry form and then moved away, she recommended asking Jacqueline for landing-page feedback. The scene shows support that includes judgment and collaboration, even before there is a settled answer.

prior_content_context.argument: When a couple schedules a tour a few weeks away, there's an opportunity to help them picture their wedding before they arrive. We look at what happens during that wait, including the emails they receive and where a personal conversation would help.
prior_content_context.audience: Venue owners investing in visibility who want to carry a couple's interest through to the in-person tour.
prior_content_context.mechanism: WIA reviewed the inquiry-to-tour journey and asked about the venue's existing virtual-tour option. Whitney proposed an earlier phone or virtual connection for couples whose in-person visit was further away. Fallon Looney, who was on the historical call and is no longer with WIA, suggested a supplemental email with wedding footage and an invitation to ask questions. The recommendations respected the owner's tour schedule rather than asking her to add more tour hours.
